prompt.context: The Carolina Symphony Orchestra (CSO) is in trouble. Despite recently doubling down on marketing and advertising, the orchestra's profitability has consistently dropped for the last several years. The executive board has enlisted your help to diagnose the cause of this nosedive and reverse it. The CSO must find a sustainable method to generate net-new profits over the next two years to hit its strategic growth goals.
prompt.question: Diagnose the root cause of CSO's declining profitability and recommend a course of action to generate at least $3M in incremental profit over the next two years.

clarifying_info.a: The CSO is the only professional symphony in the area, but it competes with other high-caliber entertainment providers. It plays mainly classical music but also incorporates some popular music.

clarifying_info.q: What products or revenue streams does the CSO have?
clarifying_info.a: CSO provides group, single, and subscription tickets, plus community education and engagement events and public concerts. Revenue is split into three categories: earned (ticket and concession sales), contributed (donations and grants), and investment (securities).

clarifying_info.q: Who is the typical CSO audience?
clarifying_info.a: The main segment consists of older, wealthier consumers, although there is a burgeoning interest among younger subscribers.

clarifying_info.q: What is the specific profit target?
clarifying_info.a: The CSO needs incremental profit of $3M over the next two years.

exhibits.title: Carolina Symphony Orchestra: Revenue & Cost (2017-2019)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing CSO total costs and three revenue streams (Earned, Contributed, Investment) for 2017, 2018, and 2019. Values are in $M, with the y-axis running from 0 to 12.
exhibits.data: Costs appear roughly flat around $10.6-11.2M across all three years. Earned Revenue shows a visible decline year-over-year. Contributed Revenue and Investment Revenue are also shown separately.

exhibits.title: Ticket Sales Data (2017-2019)
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down ticket sales by category (Single Attendance, Premium Subscription, Group) for each year, showing number of tickets sold and average ticket price.

exhibits.title: Subscriber Preferences by Segment (2019-2020)
exhibits.shows: A Harvey ball chart showing the percentage of each subscriber segment (5+ Years 31%, 1-5 Years 18%, less than 1 Year 51%) that identifies six characteristics as key drivers of patronage: Musical Selection, Number of Concerts per Season, Quality of Guest Artists, Quality of Orchestra, Programming Variety, Quality of Venue.
exhibits.data: Subscriber distribution: <1 Year = 51%, 1-5 Years = 18%, 5+ Years = 31%. Harvey balls indicate relative importance of each characteristic per segment (each ball represents ~25% of that segment).

exhibits.title: Improving Orchestra Quality: Options
exhibits.shows: A table comparing two options for improving orchestra quality — hiring a renowned conductor vs. increasing principal chair salaries — across cost per year, expected revenue in Year 1, and expected revenue in Year 2.

framework: Revenue Benchmarking: Break down revenue by type — Earned (ticket & concession: # tickets sold x price, by category), Contributed (donation size and frequency), Investment (portfolio holdings and performance)

Cost Benchmarking: Separate Fixed costs (facilities overhead, performer salaries, insurance) from Variable costs (printed materials, concessions, booking fees); determine whether costs are driving the decline
Customer Profiling: Understand distribution of ticket holders by age, income, visit frequency; assess brand awareness and product attractiveness
Competitive Analysis: Estimate CSO's market share of local live entertainment; benchmark prices vs. similar offerings; identify industry best practices vs. current strategy

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1a, what is the primary driver of the profitability decline?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe that costs are roughly stable (~$10.6M to $11.2M, a minor change), eliminating cost as the main driver. The primary driver is declining Earned Revenue, which is falling sharply year-over-year. Investment Revenue also declines but more slowly and with less overall impact. Contributed Revenue should also be assessed. Candidate should ask for a more granular revenue breakdown (Exhibit 1b) to pinpoint the exact source.

math.setup: Examine revenue categories to identify which is dropping most significantly
steps: Cost change: approximately $10.6M to $11.2M — essentially flat
Earned Revenue shows the steepest YOY decline
Investment Revenue declining but at a slower rate with smaller absolute impact
math.answer: Earned revenue (ticket sales) is the primary driver of profitability decline; costs are not the issue

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1b, calculate the revenue change for each ticket category and identify the primary driver of earned revenue decline.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total revenue per category per year (tickets x avg price) and compare. Group tickets should be quickly eliminated as a significant driver. The candidate must compare Single Attendance vs. Premium Subscription on a revenue basis, not just ticket volume. The key insight is that Premium Subscription is the single largest revenue segment and has declined the most in absolute dollar terms.

math.setup: Revenue = Number of Tickets Sold x Average Ticket Price for each category and year
math.answer: Premium Subscription is the primary driver of earned revenue decline with a total drop of ~$1.14M. Single Attendance fell $140K. Group tickets are not a significant driver. Second-order insight: both subscription price and volume are falling simultaneously, suggesting adverse price signaling or that the pricing lever is not the core problem.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2a, which subscriber preference should CSO prioritize to recover subscription revenue?
questions.guidance: Good candidates identify Quality of Guest Artists and Quality of Orchestra as the top two Harvey ball factors. Excellent candidates go further and calculate a weighted score across subscriber segments to show Orchestra Quality is mathematically the most valued attribute. Weighting matters because the majority (51%) are newer subscribers (<1 year).

math.setup: Weighted score = sum of (Harvey ball value x segment share) for each attribute. Harvey ball values: full = 1.0, three-quarter = 0.75, half = 0.5, quarter = 0.25, empty = 0. Segment weights: <1 Year = 0.51, 1-5 Years = 0.18, 5+ Years = 0.31.
math.answer: Quality of Orchestra scores 73.75 vs. Guest Artists 65.5 — Orchestra Quality is the mathematically more impactful driver and should be prioritized.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2b and a discount rate of 10%, calculate the NPV of each option and determine which meets the $3M profit threshold.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize both options require the same NPV calculation structure (net cash flow each year discounted at 10%). Excellent candidates spot that both options yield the same NPV and therefore the choice should be justified on qualitative grounds. Both options exceed the $3M threshold on a combined 2-year NPV basis.

math.setup: NPV = (Revenue_yr1 - Cost_yr1)/1.10 + (Revenue_yr2 - Cost_yr2)/1.10^2. The cost is an ongoing annual expense.
math.answer: Both options yield NPV of ~$3.02M over two years, meeting the $3M threshold. The options are financially equivalent; the choice must be made on qualitative grounds.

brainstorming.prompt: The board agrees that the subscription ticket holder category is mainly to blame for the eroding bottom line. What levers could the board pull to boost the revenue generated by its subscription-holding patrons?

categories.name: Understand the Consumer Base
ideas: Profile demographic of subscription holders (age range, income level, family status)
Analyze visit frequency and purchasing history of existing subscribers

categories.name: Survey and Research
ideas: Survey subscription holders to identify key drivers of purchasing behavior (e.g., programming, special guest artists)

categories.name: Targeted Marketing
ideas: Launch targeted social media campaigns to re-engage lapsed subscribers
Deploy direct mail to former subscription holders
Partner with local media or cultural institutions to raise awareness

categories.name: Product and Benefit Enhancement
ideas: Expand concert offerings within subscription packages
Add exclusive perks (e.g., lounge access, backstage tours, soloist meet-and-greets)
Develop tiered subscription levels to capture different willingness-to-pay segments

categories.name: Pricing Strategy
ideas: Consider a modest price increase to reverse potential negative price signaling (prior price cuts may have signaled declining quality)
Avoid further price slashing given that current management has already been cutting prices without success

recommendation: The CSO should invest in improving Orchestra Quality — the most mathematically valued attribute among subscribers — by choosing one of the two board-identified options. Both options yield approximately the same NPV (~$3.02M), which meets the $3M threshold. The preferred choice should be justified qualitatively: Option 1 (Renowned Conductor) provides immediate brand visibility and may inspire the orchestra to higher musicianship, making it well-suited if rapid subscriber re-engagement is the priority. Option 2 (Principal Chair Salaries) offers more stable, controllable cost structure and long-term talent retention, making it preferable if sustainable quality improvement is the goal.
Either option meets the financial target; candidate should pick one and defend it clearly with reference to the $3M goal and qualitative tradeoffs.
risks: Projected revenue figures for both options may prove inaccurate — subscriber uptake depends on how well the improvement resonates with the varied preference distribution across segments
Option 1 (Conductor): the search process may be costly and time-consuming; the musical community may reject the orchestra's choice
Option 2 (Salaries): the orchestra may already employ best-in-class principal chairs; salary increases for one group may create a domino effect on other musicians
Broader risk: declining subscription trends may reflect factors beyond orchestra quality (e.g., broader demographic shifts, digital entertainment competition) that these options alone cannot address
next_steps: Option 1: Formally announce the conductor search and hire an industry headhunter to lead a targeted national or international search
Option 2: Assess all principal chair salaries, review past audition and performance records, and determine how increases should be distributed to maximize impact
Both options: conduct internal benchmarking against comparable orchestras to verify the validity of the projected revenue figures
Both options: implement a subscriber survey to track preference changes and validate that orchestra quality improvements are driving renewed subscriptions
